message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – originally for drawing pixels, now also for massively parallel compute tasks. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32) with very powerful, complex control logic, large caches, and sophisticated branch prediction. | Hundreds to thousands of simpler cores optimized for throughput; each core is lightweight and shares a large pool of registers. |
| **Instruction set** | Complex instruction set (CISC) or reduced instruction set (RISC) with many features (branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution). | Very simple, SIMD‑style instructions; each core executes the same instruction on many data elements simultaneously. |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, high bandwidth memory access, low latency. | Shared memory pools, high bandwidth but higher latency; often uses GDDR or HBM memory. |
| **Typical workloads** | Serial or lightly parallel tasks: OS, web browsers, office apps, database queries, etc. | Highly parallel tasks: rendering frames, scientific simulations, machine‑learning inference/training, video encoding/decoding. |
| **Performance characteristics** | High single‑thread performance, low latency. | High throughput for many threads, lower per‑thread performance. |
| **Programming model** | Traditional CPU programming (C/C++, Java, etc.) with multi‑threading. | GPU programming requires parallel kernels (CUDA, OpenCL, Vulkan, Metal, DirectX 12, etc.). |
| **Energy efficiency** | Optimized for low power per core when idle, but can consume a lot of power under heavy load. | Optimized for high throughput per watt; GPUs can be more power‑hungry but deliver more work per watt for parallel tasks. |

### Why the difference matters

- **Serial vs. Parallel**: CPUs excel at tasks that require complex decision making and branching. GPUs shine when you can break a problem into many identical operations that can run in parallel.
- **Latency vs. Throughput**: CPUs aim for low latency (quick response to a single request). GPUs aim for high throughput (processing many requests simultaneously).
- **Flexibility vs. Specialization**: CPUs are general‑purpose; GPUs are specialized but increasingly used for general compute (GPGPU).

In practice, modern systems use both: the CPU handles most of the operating system and application logic, while the GPU accelerates graphics and compute‑heavy workloads. This synergy allows devices—from smartphones to supercomputers—to perform efficiently across a wide range of tasks.
